1. Course map, sources, and how to use this guide
This study guide continues the series of guides for the course Introduction to Engi-
neering (code CC-INEN010104, 4 ECTS, fall semester 2026/27, Tashkent University
of Technology, Faculty of Power Engineering) and covers weeks 5–7: Problem Fram-
ing and Modelling II (week 5), Quantitative Reasoning I (week 6) and Quantitative
Reasoning II (week 7). Every savol (savollar
• questions), topshiriq (topshiriqlar — assignments), atama (atamalar — terms),
formula (formulalar) and qoida (qoidalar — rules) of these weeks, encountered
in the lectures, labs and templates, is written out in full and supplied with a
model answer or solution. The guide is structured so that you can prepare for
the weekly mini projects (30%), the midterm (30%)and the final (40%) without
re-watching hundreds of slides.
The course is taught by Dr. Mohammad Reza Bahrami (lectures; Faculty of Power
Engineering, PhD Mechanical Engineering) and Ibrokhimjon Khamidov (labs; lab in-
structor; research interests — lean manufacturing, sustainability, quantitative as-
sessment of productivity). The course follows a Project-Based Learning approach:
all semester work revolves around a single team system selected in week 2. Week
5 ends with a team deliverable, Milestone 2 — a problem-framing document and an
explicit list of modelling assumptions; labs 5–7 keep working with the same ten sce-
nario cards as Lab 4. Lectures 5–7 draw on P. Kosky, R. Balmer, W. Keat, G. Wise,
“Exploring Engineering” (5th ed.): chapter 2 — the Need-Know-How-Solve method,
units in square brackets, significant figures and order-of-magnitude estimates (Ex-
amples 2.3–2.4, Problem 10); chapter 4 — models and “beware of your assumptions”
(Example 4.8); chapter 8
• highway capacity as an intensity; chapter 10 — the electric circuit model.
How to use this guide: sections 2–4 follow the week-by-week chronology; within each
week there is first a digest of “all the qoidalar of the week” (what gets tested first
of all), then all the savollar of the lecture and the lab with model answers, then the
lab’s topshiriqlar with solutions and a glossary of atamalar. Sections 5–8 are sum-
mary sections: all the formulas (Formulalar), all the rules (Qoidalar), all the assign-
ments (Topshiriqlar) and a cheat sheet of key facts. The terminology is kept bilingual
(Russian + English) because the exam is administered in English; the numbers in all
examples are illustrative values from the course slides, not measured data. Week
8 is the Midterm Assessment: a written, paper-based test covering the first seven
weeks.

2. Week 5 — Problem framing and
modelling II (Problem Framing and Modelling II)
2.1
2.1. Key statements (“all the qoidalar” of week 5)
The week 5 lecture turns the framed problem into a simple model and teaches you
to state what it assumes.
A recap of week 4 “in one breath”: sort the evidence
into fact, inference, speculation and opinion; needs, not solutions — a good problem
statement does not name a device; variables are measurable quantities with units
(performance, design, context); performance is defined by the stakeholders — write
it down in numbers.
A model is a purposeful simplification
A model is a simplified representation of a real system, built to answer a specific ques-
tion. Every model keeps something in (for the question of a bus’s range — battery
energy, distance, consumption per kilometre), throws something away (the colour of
the bus, the number of seats, the exact shape of every turn) and always has a purpose
— a question: “is one charge enough for a day on the route?”.
The lecture’s opening example is one campus electrical network and two maps.
The one-line diagram (Map A) answers connectivity questions: which buildings lose

power if the library feeder is switched off; where to place a switch; which switch
isolates a fault; it omits distances, cable cross-sections and time. The geographic
diagram (Map B) answers location questions: how long the cable to the workshop
is, which lines cross the river or the road, which building is closer to the substation;
it omits switching, protection and power ratings. Neither map is the network itself:
each is a model, a simplified picture for one type of question. The week’s epigraph
is the statistician George Box: “All models are wrong, but some are useful.”
[Source: Lecture05, slides 2, 4–7]
Four types of models
The course distinguishes four types. Physical — a real copy: a scaled-down or sim-
plified object, for example a wind turbine blade tested in a wind tunnel. Graphical
— a diagram: a drawing of parts and connections, for example a one-line diagram
or the energy-flow diagram of a car. Mathematical — equations: relations between
variables, for example Ohm’s law and the power law for an electric circuit. Com-
putational — a calculation: rules executed step by step on a computer, for example
a table of hourly electricity demand. Real projects mix several types: a diagram to
organise, equations to compute, a table
• to run the numbers.
One system — three models (campus electricity supply): the one-line diagram (graph-
ical; answers “which buildings lose power when a feeder is switched off?”; omits dis-
tances, power ratings, time); the energy balance supply = demand + losses (math-
ematical; answers “does daily generation cover daily demand?”; omits the hour in
which demand arises); the hourly demand table (computational; answers “in which
hour does the peak occur?”; omits the network diagram and the voltages). One sys-
tem, three models — the question decides which one to use.
[Source: Lecture05, slides 8–9; Lab5, p. 3]
Anatomy of a model: four parts
Every model consists of four parts. Inputs — what we feed in: the values we choose
or can change (battery size, speed, route length). Parameters
• — what is kept fixed: the numbers describing the system and its conditions (en-
ergy consumption per kilometre, the usable share of the battery). Relationships
— the rules: equations or steps that link the numbers (Energy = energy per km
× distance). Outputs — what the model predicts: the results we evaluate (range
in km, energy in kWh/day). “A model
• is a machine: numbers go in, a rule is applied, numbers come out” (A model is
a machine). Every number needs its own units.
The week 4 variables become the roles of the model: performance variables →out-
puts (range per charge [km], energy per day [kWh/day]); design variables →inputs
(battery capacity [kWh], number of buses); context variables →parameters (route
length [km], air temperature [°C], hours on depot charging). Last week’s list of vari-
ables is already the skeleton of this week’s model.
[Source: Lecture05, slides 13–14; Lab5, p. 4]

Need–Know–How–Solve and the first bus model
The week’s method is Need–Know–How–Solve (Kosky, ch. 2): Need — the variable
we want (range per charge, km); Know — what is already known (battery capacity,
usable share, consumption per km, route length); How — the model and the assump-
tions (Range = usable energy ÷ energy per km); Solve — compute, check the units,
interpret. Kosky stresses that How also includes the assumptions you make in or-
der to solve the problem. Week 4 gave the Need; week 5 builds the How — and the
assumptions hidden inside it.
The first model is an electric campus bus: trip energy E = e × d, range R = (u × C)
÷ e, where C is the battery capacity [kWh], u is the usable share (unitless), e is the
consumption [kWh/km], d
• is the distance [km], R [km], E [kWh]. A unit check after Kosky: (u × C) [kWh]
÷ e [kWh/km] = R [km].
E = e × d [kWh] = [kWh/km] × [km]
R = (u × C) ÷ e →160 [kWh] ÷ 1,2 [kWh/km] = 133 [km]
[Source: Lecture05, slides 15–16; method: Kosky, ch. 2]
The model’s numbers: 160 kWh, 133 km, 96 km

Substituting the numbers (illustrative, not data): usable energy u×C = 0, 8×200 kWh
= 160 kWh; range R = 160 kWh ÷ 1,2 kWh/km = 133 km; the daily requirement is 8
laps ×12km =
96 km. The model says: one charge covers the day with a margin of about 37 km.
But how far can this number be trusted? That depends on the assumptions.
[Source: Lecture05, slide 17]
Three kinds of assumptions and a template for writing them
Simplifying — what we ignore: hills, traffic lights, stops, differences between drivers.
Data — what we fix: e = 1, 2 kWh/km; C = 200 kWh, u = 0, 8. Boundary — what we
leave outside: the passengers, the charger and the grid; only the bus is in the model.
The idea of week 2 repeats: the boundary is a choice, and every assumption is a
choice too.
The course template: “We assume [assumption] because [reason].
If it is wrong,
[effect on the result]”. Example: “We assume 1,2 kWh/km in all seasons, because
we only have autumn test data. If it is wrong, the winter range may fall below the
daily requirement of 96 km”. A quick check: will a teammate be able to understand
what you ignored, fixed and left outside? Can it be checked? An assumption that is
written down can be checked.
A hidden one cannot.

Hidden assumptions and their price
None of the hidden assumptions of the bus model is written in the equation. e = 1, 2
kWh/km — “the same in every season”: cabin heating raises e, and the range drops.
“The route is flat, the load is similar”: hills and full buses spend more energy. u×C =
160 kWh — “the battery never loses capacity”: an ageing battery stores less. “We
start from a full battery”: depot charging always works; a missed charge cuts the
day short. This is exactly why assumptions are written down.
One model — different assumptions: base case 133 km; full passenger load 114 km;
old battery 107 km; winter heating 89 km; winter + old battery 71 km (cases: e =
1, 4and1, 8 kWh/km, usable energy 128 kWh). The daily requirement is 96 km: the
base case, the full load and the old battery cover the day; winter heating and “winter
+ old battery” no longer do. Conclusion: “one charge covers the day” holds only for
as long as the assumptions hold.
A solar example of the same idea: the hidden assumption “the sun shines at full
power all day”. The naive model: 5 kW ×24h = 120 kWh per day; the clear-day profile
is about 31 kWh per day. The naive model is nearly four times too high. Note the
units: kW is power, kWh is energy. Before trusting a number, ask what conditions it
silently assumes.
[Source: Lecture05, slides 20–22]
Is the model good enough? (Fit for purpose)
Three verdicts. Too simple (too simple) — it misses what matters: R = 160 ÷ 1,2 for
every day of the year; winter, hills and ageing are invisible. Fit for purpose (fit for
purpose) — it answers the question: separate consumption for summer and winter
plus a safety margin; enough to decide whether one charge covers the day.
Too
detailed (too detailed) — it cannot be built and checked: battery chemistry, every
traffic light, every driver’s habits; it needs data that do not exist. The rule:
choose the simplest model that answers the question well enough to make a
decision.
When a model misleads: the range model (e = 1, 2kWh/km) was built for mild autumn
test days but is used during a winter cold snap — heating raises e, and the range is
overestimated; the solar generation profile was built for a clear summer day but is
used in a cloudy winter week — generation falls far below the profile; the dormitory
load of 2 kW is for mild weather but is used in a week of hard frost — the load is far
above 2 kW. Every model has a range within which its assumptions are valid. Know
it and state it.
[Source: Lecture05, slides 27, 29]
Three checks and the “build — check — revise” loop
Three sanity checks: (1) units — (u × C) [kWh] ÷ e [kWh/km] gives km, so the range
has the right unit; (2) order of magnitude — are 133 km plausible for a city bus: tens–
hundreds of km, not 3 km and not 3 000 km; (3) a known value — does the result
agree with a datasheet, a test drive or last month’s logs. Kosky ends the energy
example with the question “Is this a reasonable answer?” — ask it every time.
The week’s cycle: Frame (the problem statement and the variables) →Build (a first
simple model with units) →Check (units, magnitude, known values) →Revise (fix
the assumptions; add detail only if needed) — repeat until it is good enough for
the decision. A preview: in week 11 the sensitivity analysis will ask “what if this
assumption is wrong — and by how much?”
[Source: Lecture05, slides 28, 30–31]

2.2. Savollar of week 5 — lecture and lab questions with model
answers
S1. What is a model? Why does the lecture insist that “no map is the net-
work”?
Answer. A model is a simplified representation of a real system, built to answer a
specific question. The lecture’s example: one campus electrical network and two
maps — the one-line diagram (connectivity questions: which buildings lose power
when a feeder is switched off, where to place a switch, which switch isolates a fault)
and the geographic diagram (location questions: the cable length to the workshop,
crossings of the river or the road, the building closest to the substation). Neither map
is the network: each is a model, a simplified picture made for one type of question.
George Box’s epigraph: “All models are wrong, but some are useful”.
S2. Lecture interactive “Match the Question to the Model”: which type of
model fits each of the six questions A–F best, and why?
Answer. A (range on a single charge) — mathematical: energy = consumption per
km × distance set against the battery’s energy. B (which buildings lose power when
a feeder is switched off) — graphical: the one-line diagram shows which feeder sup-
plies a building. C (dormitory temperature over a day) — computational: we step
through the hours. D (a turbine blade in a strong wind) — physical: the blade in a
wind tunnel. E (where passengers stand at a busy stop) — graphical: a sketch of the
stop. F (a building’s energy over a day) — mathematical: kW ×h = kWh from the
loads. Several types may fit — explain why.
S3. What four parts does every model consist of? Give an example of each
for the electric bus.
Answer. Inputs — what we feed in and can change: battery size, speed, route length.
Parameters
• — what is kept fixed: consumption per km, the usable share of the battery. Rela-
tionships — the rules linking the numbers: Energy = energy per km × distance.
Outputs — the predictions we evaluate: range [km], energy per day [kWh/day].
The lecture’s formula: “a model is a machine: numbers go in, a rule is applied,
numbers come out”, and every number needs its own units.
S4. How do the week 4 variables (performance, design, context) become the
roles of the model?
Answer. Performance variables become the outputs: range per charge [km], energy
per day [kWh/day].
Design variables become the inputs: battery capacity [kWh],
number of buses. Context variables become the parameters: route length [km], out-
side temperature [°C], hours on depot charging. Last week’s list of variables is al-
ready the skeleton of this week’s model: a variable’s role is determined by how it
enters the calculation.
S5. Apply Need–Know–How–Solve to the bus range question.
Answer. Need — the variable we want: range per charge [km]. Know — what is
known: battery capacity, usable share, consumption per km, route length. How —
the model and the assumptions: Range = usable energy ÷ energy per km, i.e. R =
(u×C) ÷ e; after Kosky, How also includes the assumptions made in order to solve the
problem. Solve — compute, check the units, interpret: (u × C) [kWh] ÷ e [kWh/km]
= R [km]. Week 4 gave the Need; week 5 builds the How — and the assumptions
hidden inside it.

S6. Substitute the numbers into the bus model: what are the usable energy,
the range and the daily requirement?
Answer. Usable energy u × C = 0, 8 × 200 kWh = 160 kWh. Range R = 160 kWh ÷ 1,2
kWh/km = 133 km. Daily requirement: 8 laps ×12km = 96 km. The model’s conclusion:
one charge covers the day with a margin of about 37 km. The lecture immediately
warns: how far the number can be trusted depends on the assumptions; the values
are illustrative, not measured data.
S7. Which three kinds of assumptions does the course distinguish? Give an
example of each for the bus model.
Answer. Simplifying — what we ignore: hills, traffic lights, stops, differences be-
tween drivers.
Data assumptions — what we fix: e = 1, 2 kWh/km; C = 200 kWh,
u = 0, 8. Boundary — what we leave outside the model: the passengers, the charger,
the grid; only the bus is in the model. Every assumption is a choice (like the system
boundary from week 2), and each is written down with the template: “We assume . . .
because . . .. If it is wrong, . . .”.
S8.
Lecture exercise “Spot the Hidden Assumptions”: find the hidden as-
sumption in the statement “The dormitory needs a 2 kW heater, so a day
costs 48 kWh” and rewrite it with the template.
Answer.
The hidden assumption: the heater runs at full power for all 24 hours,
regardless of the weather. Rewrite: “We assume the heater is always on, because
we have no thermostat data. If it switches off in cycles, the energy is below 48 kWh”.
Similarly: “3 000 kWh per day →90000 kWh over 30 days” — the assumption “every
day is an average day”: if winter days consume more, the month will exceed 90 000.
“1,2 kWh/km →ten buses over a 12 km lap each = 144 kWh” — the assumptions
“consumption is the same for all” and “one lap each”: if some laps are full, the total
will exceed 144 kWh.
S9. How does the range change under full passenger load, an old battery and
winter heating?
Answer. Base case — 133 km; full passenger load — 114 km; old battery — 107 km;
winter heating — 89 km; winter + old battery — 71 km (cases: e = 1, 4and1, 8 kWh/km,
usable energy 128 kWh). The daily requirement is 96 km: the first three cases cover
the day; winter heating and “winter + old battery” do not. The lecture’s moral: “one
charge covers the day” holds only for as long as the assumptions hold.
S10. Why is the naive estimate of a solar array, 5 kW ×24h = 120 kWh/day,
nearly four times too high?
Answer. The hidden assumption is “the sun shines at full power all day”. The naive
model gives 5 kW ×24h = 120 kWh per day; the clear-day profile is about 31 kWh
per day, i.e. nearly four times less. The lesson: before trusting a number, ask what
conditions it silently assumes. And keep the units apart: kW is power, kWh is energy.
S11. What does “fit for purpose” mean, and what are the two opposite ways
a model can fail?
Answer. Fit for purpose — the model is good enough to answer the question and make
a decision. The “too simple” failure: R = 160 ÷ 1,2 for every day of the year — winter,
hills and ageing are invisible. The “too detailed” failure: battery chemistry, every
traffic light, every driver’s habits — the model cannot be built or checked, and needs
inaccessible data. A fit-for-purpose model — for example, separate consumption for
summer and winter plus a safety margin — is enough to decide whether one charge
covers the day. The rule: choose the simplest model that answers the question well
enough to make a decision.

S12. Which three sanity checks does a model pass, and when does a model
“mislead”?
Answer. The checks: (1) units — (u × C) [kWh] ÷ e [kWh/km] gives km; (2) order
of magnitude — 133 km is plausible for a city bus (tens–hundreds of km, not 3 and
not 3 000); (3) a known value — a datasheet, a test drive, last month’s logs. A model
misleads outside the range of its assumptions: the autumn range model — in a winter
cold snap; the clear summer day profile — in a cloudy winter week; the 2 kW load for
mild weather — in a frosty week. Every model has a range in which its assumptions
are valid: know it and state it.
S13. Lab 5: what does the assessed team work consist of (ten steps), and
how is it graded?
Answer.
The team takes the same scenario card as in Lab 4 and, in 45 minutes,
works through ten steps: (1) the model’s question; (2) the type, with justification; (3)
the anatomy — inputs, parameters, relationships, outputs, all with units; (4) Need–
Know–How–Solve; (5) at least six assumptions using the template; (6) labelling Safe /
Risky / Need Data; (7) changing one assumption and the effect on the output; (8) the
checks — units, order of magnitude, a known value; (9) the verdict Too Simple / Fit
for Purpose / Too Detailed; (10) a revision and the need for data. Grading per step:
3/2/1/0 (fully / partially / almost nothing / missing); the steps go in order — each next
one depends on the previous ones.
S14. Lab 5, model answer “EV Charging & Battery Test Station”: what are
the model’s question, type, anatomy and result? What happens on switching
to 50 kW fast charging?
Answer. The question: will the station’s peak power stay within the grid operator’s
150 kW limit in the busiest hour? Type — mathematical. Anatomy: inputs — the
chargers in use n [units], the power of one charger P₁ [kW]; parameters — the limit
L = 150 kW, 4 chargers; the relationship P = n × P₁, compliant if P ≤L; outputs —
P [kW], yes/no. Solve: P = 4 × 22 = 88 kW ≤150 kW. A stress test: at P₁ = 50 kW,
P = 4 × 50 = 200 kW — above the limit; the model exposes a hidden violation. Verdict:
Fit for Purpose; the revision — a measured diversity factor instead of the worst case;
the data item — a week of measurements per charger.
[Source: Lecture05; Lab5 — lecture and lab questions of week 5]

The baseline changes the story
One fact: the LED retrofit saves 12 kW. Two true percentages: 60% of corridor light-
ing (12 ÷ 20 kW) and 7% of the building’s peak (12 ÷ 180 kW). Different baselines
and boundaries give different but true stories. Always ask: a percentage of what?
Misleading comparisons need no false number — each needs a question. Different
denominators: “Route A has fewer complaints” (it has far fewer passengers) — ask
“per what?”. Cherry-picked days: “the best week of the semester” — “which days
were dropped?”. A truncated axis: a bar chart starting at 80 turns a 5% gap into a
huge one — “where does the axis start?”. Four questions for any interpretation: (1)
for which decision is this number? (2) which metric fits the decision — the mean, the
peak, a percentile, the worst case? (3) which baseline, boundary and time basis are
used? (4) which assumption, if it turned out wrong, would flip the conclusion? Ask
them before accepting a result, and before presenting it.

• The model’s verdict: Too Simple / Fit for Purpose / Too Detailed; the goal is fit
for purpose: the simplest
model that answers the question well enough to decide.
• Finish with one revision and one additional need for data.
• Every model has a range in which its assumptions are valid: know it and state
it.
6.3
6.3. Rules of quantitative reasoning
• Demand is what the system must deliver; capacity is the maximum it can deliver;
both need
units and a time basis.
• A number without a time basis is as incomplete as a number without units.
• Compare like with like: one unit and one time basis on both sides before
dividing.
• Utilisation = demand ÷ capacity: below ~{}0,8 — comfortable; around 1 —
tight; above 1 —
demand is turned away or a queue grows.
• Size for the peak, not for the average: the average hides the peak (a 94 kW
average against a 180 kW peak at
13:00).
• kW is an intensity, kWh is an amount; power × time = energy.
• Carry the units in square brackets: 60 [kW] ×2 [h] = 120 [kWh]; the units check
both the method
and the answer.
• Change in stock = inflow −outflow; when positive, something is accumulating
(a queue, a buffer,
a battery).

• The flow rules (flow = speed × density; number inside = arrivals × time) hold
only under
steady-state conditions.
• The bottleneck is the stage with the smallest capacity; it sets the system’s max-
imum practical
throughput.
• Estimate before calculating: identify the quantity and its units →break into
factors →round
each factor to one digit and multiply →check the units and compare with a known
value.
• An order-of-magnitude estimate is correct to within a factor of ~{}10 and often
better: 21 barbershops
against 23 in the directory.
• Bound the estimate: low / typical / high; if the decision does not change across
the range —
stop refining (23–38kW →still “a rooftop installation”).
• Precise is not the same as correct: one–two significant figures; “about 30 kW”,
not “29,17 kW”.
• Most estimation errors are errors of units or of counting: confusing kW and
kWh, the forgotten peak,
double counting, false precision.
• When an answer looks strange, check the units and the time basis first (0, 2MW =
200 kW; 36 min = 0, 6h).
6.4
6.4.
Rules for working with incomplete data and making deci-
sions
• Name the data problem first: too little, missing, noisy, out of date / unrepresen-
tative, wrong
definition / unit — the fix depends on the type.
• Five sources of numbers: measure, look up, ask, estimate, analogy — with dif-
ferent levels of trust;
write the source and the confidence next to every number.
48

Introduction to Engineering — Weeks 5–7: study guide
·
• Use ranges, not single numbers: recompute the main result for the low,
typical and high values.
• A range tells the reader how far to trust the answer: “about 100 to 145 km”.
• With a small sample, write n next to every number; do not claim more than n
points can show.
• One odd value moves the mean a lot, and the median almost not at all; choose
the metric
deliberately.
• Triangulate: estimate an important quantity by at least two independent routes;
agreement
builds trust, disagreement points to where to look.
• The same numbers support different readings, and all can be true; ask for
which decision this number is.
• The decision chooses the metric, not the other way round: the median — the
typical case; the mean — the total
load; the 90th percentile — the unlucky; the maximum — the worst case.
• Always ask: a percentage of what?
Different baselines and boundaries give
different but true
stories (60% against 7%).
• A result above 100% is a hint that the baseline boundary is wrong; use one
boundary
before and after the change, and state it.
• Misleading comparisons need no false number: different denominators (“per
what?”),
cherry-picked days (“which days were dropped?”), a truncated axis (“where does the
axis start?”).
• Four questions for any interpretation: for which decision? which metric? which
base, boundary
and time basis? which assumption would flip the conclusion?

• An honest report: result + range + top assumption + what would change the
conclusion.
• Low confidence goes on the page: hiding it does not remove it.
• Find the flip point: the threshold at which the decision changes (the break-even
premium ≈the annual
saving × years of service).
